questions.stem: In discussing literature, what does the term 'values' most accurately refer to?
options: The beliefs and principles about what matters that a person or group holds
The number of characters an author chooses to include in a story
The literal meaning of unfamiliar words as listed in a dictionary
The commercial worth of a book based on how many copies it sells
questions.explanation: Values are the beliefs and priorities about what is important or right, and literary texts can reveal the values of characters, authors and communities. 'The literal meaning of unfamiliar words' confuses values with vocabulary or denotation, which is about word meaning rather than belief. A useful cue: values answer the question 'what does this person think matters?'
questions.teaching:
When literary study uses this term, it does not mean numerical worth or how much something costs.

It means the beliefs and principles a person, group or society holds about what matters — loyalty, honesty, family, independence, obedience, success. Texts embody them, sometimes deliberately and sometimes without noticing, and different eras and cultures hold different ones. That is why a text can seem to endorse something a modern reader finds troubling, and why identifying whose beliefs a text reflects is a standard analytical move.

questions.stem: A text's 'point of view' in the sense of ideas and issues means:
options: The number of narrators the text uses across its chapters
The order in which events are arranged in the plot
The attitude or stance the text takes towards an issue
The physical location from which a scene is described
questions.explanation: When we discuss ideas, issues and points of view, point of view means the attitude or position a text conveys about a topic. 'The physical location from which a scene is described' confuses this with visual perspective or camera angle, which is a different use of the word. Ask yourself whether you are describing where the narrator stands or what the text seems to believe.
questions.teaching:
The phrase 'point of view' means two different things in English, and questions exploit the ambiguity.

In one sense it is technical, describing who narrates and how much they know — first person, third person limited, and so on. In the other sense it means the stance the text takes on an issue: what it seems to approve of, criticise or assume. The second sense is about ideas rather than narration, so a text can have a first-person narrator and take a stance the narrator does not share. Read which sense the question is using.

questions.stem: Why does knowing the historical context of a novel help a reader explain its representation of values?
options: It reveals the beliefs and conditions of the time that shaped the ideas in the text
It proves the events described in the novel actually happened as written
It shows that the author's values must match those of every character
It guarantees that readers today will share the attitudes shown in the text
questions.explanation: Context supplies the social conditions, beliefs and debates of the period, which helps explain why particular ideas and attitudes appear in a text. 'It proves the events actually happened' is wrong because context does not make fiction factual. Context explains why ideas are present, not that events are true.

questions.stem: Which statement about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander literature is accurate?
options: It presents a single unified viewpoint shared by all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
It is always set in the distant past rather than in contemporary Australia
It is written only for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers and no others
It comes from many distinct language groups and Countries, so it represents diverse perspectives
questions.explanation: There are hundreds of distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander nations, languages and Countries, so their literature carries a wide range of perspectives, forms and concerns. 'A single unified viewpoint' is false and treats many peoples as one group. Watch for any option that flattens diversity into one voice.

questions.stem: A short story shows a teenage character refusing a well-paid job in the city to stay and care for an ageing grandparent on a remote property. What value is this choice most clearly representing?
options: That paid employment has no importance to any of the characters
That obligation to family outweighs individual financial advancement
That rural life is economically superior to working in a city
That teenagers are incapable of making independent decisions
questions.explanation: The character sacrifices money for a relative, so the text foregrounds family duty as more important than personal gain. 'Rural life is economically superior' misreads the choice, since the story shows the character giving up income rather than gaining it. Track what a character gives up to see what they value most.

questions.stem: Two Australian novels written eighty years apart both describe a drought. The older one presents the land as an enemy to be beaten; the newer one presents it as a living system to be cared for. What is the best explanation?
options: The older author simply had less accurate scientific information about droughts
The newer novel must be fiction while the older one must be non-fiction
Descriptions of setting cannot carry values, so the difference is only stylistic
Each text reflects attitudes to land available in its own social and historical context
questions.explanation: Representations of land are shaped by the beliefs circulating when a text was written, so the contrast shows shifting social attitudes rather than a random difference. 'The older author had less accurate scientific information' is tempting but wrong, because the difference is one of attitude and value, not factual error about weather. Ask what belief a description invites, not whether it is scientifically precise.

questions.stem: Which sentence best explains how a text represents the values of a group rather than just one person?
options: The novel was widely read and reviewed favourably in several major newspapers
The community's repeated welcoming of strangers presents hospitality as a shared obligation
The protagonist alone decides to welcome a stranger, surprising everyone in the village
The narrator describes the village square in detail across three long paragraphs
questions.explanation: Group values show up in shared, repeated behaviour and in what a community treats as expected, so a pattern of collective hospitality points to a group value. 'The protagonist alone decides to welcome a stranger, surprising everyone' shows an individual acting against the group, which is evidence of a personal value instead. Look for repetition across characters when arguing for group values.

questions.stem: 'All night the wind clawed at the tin roof and muttered under the door.' Which literary device is used?
options: Onomatopoeia, because the words imitate the sounds they describe
Personification, because the wind is given human and animal actions
Simile, because the wind is compared to something using 'like' or 'as'
Hyperbole, because the sentence deliberately exaggerates for comic effect
questions.explanation: 'Clawed' and 'muttered' are actions of living creatures applied to a non-living thing, which is personification. Simile is the common trap, but a simile requires an explicit comparison word such as 'like' or 'as', and there is none here. Cue: look for a comparison word before calling something a simile; if a thing is simply *doing* something living, it is personification.

questions.stem: A novel opens: 'He waited. Boots on gravel. Closer. He did not breathe.' What does this sentence patterning most likely contribute to the style?
options: A leisurely, reflective mood that invites the reader to consider the setting
A formal, academic tone that distances the reader from the character
A comic tone that signals the danger is not meant to be believed
A tense, urgent pace that holds the reader in the character's moment of fear
questions.explanation: Very short sentences and fragments give the reader little information at a time, which quickens the reading pace and mirrors the character's held breath. The 'leisurely, reflective mood' option describes the effect of long, flowing sentences with several clauses, so it reverses the actual relationship between sentence length and pace. Cue: short sentences speed a passage up; long ones slow it down.

questions.stem: Which statement is the strongest supported opinion about a text's style?
options: The storm scenes are the best part of the novel and readers will definitely enjoy them most
The novel is about a family arguing during bad weather before finally reaching an understanding
The author clearly grew up somewhere stormy, which is why the weather is described so often
The repeated storm imagery makes the family's arguments feel unavoidable, as if the conflict is weather
questions.explanation: A supported opinion names a specific feature (the repeated storm imagery) and explains the effect it creates for the reader. Saying the storm scenes are 'the best part' is tempting because it sounds like an opinion, but it only reports enjoyment and offers no feature or effect, so it cannot be discussed or challenged. Cue: a usable opinion about style always links a choice to an effect.

questions.stem: In a short story, a character's dialogue is written as: 'Reckon we'll be right, mate — she's not that far.' What does this choice of language most contribute to?
options: The story's setting, by proving exactly which year the events are taking place in
The narration's reliability, by showing the narrator is deliberately misleading the reader
The character's voice, by suggesting a relaxed, colloquial Australian way of speaking
The text's structure, by signalling that the narrative is about to move backwards in time
questions.explanation: Colloquial and idiomatic word choices in dialogue build voice — the reader hears a particular person with a particular background and manner. The setting option is tempting because dialect can hint at place, but casual expressions like these cannot pin down a specific year, so the claim is false as written. Cue: dialect and idiom in dialogue point first to voice and characterisation.

questions.stem: A novel begins: 'You wake in a room you do not recognise. The door is closed. You do not remember closing it.' What does this narrative choice contribute to the style?
options: It places the reader inside the character's confusion, creating immediacy and unease
It shows the events are being recalled long afterwards by an older narrator
It makes the narration omniscient, giving the reader access to every character's thoughts
It confirms the character is speaking directly to another character in the room
questions.explanation: Second person combined with present tense addresses the reader as the one experiencing events, which collapses the distance between reader and character and heightens immediacy. The 'recalled long afterwards' option is tempting because many novels are retrospective, but present-tense verbs ('wake', 'is', 'remember') locate the action now, not in recollection. Cue: check the tense of the verbs before deciding when the story is being told.

questions.stem: Two students disagree about a thriller in which many paragraphs are only one line long. Which response is the most defensible opinion about this stylistic choice?
options: The one-line paragraphs prove the writer ran out of material and could not develop the ideas properly
The one-line paragraphs cannot be judged at all, because opinions about style are purely personal taste
The one-line paragraphs isolate each new detail, slowing the eye and building suspense between revelations
The one-line paragraphs are a punctuation error, since a paragraph must contain at least three sentences
questions.explanation: A defensible opinion identifies the feature and reasons about the effect it has on the reader's experience, which is exactly what linking isolated paragraphs to suspense does. The 'punctuation error' option is tempting because students are often taught to develop paragraphs fully, but there is no rule requiring three sentences, and single-line paragraphs are a recognised stylistic device. Cue: an opinion about style must argue from effect, not from an invented rule.

questions.stem: When discussing the style of a literary text, which of these is an example of a text structure choice rather than a language feature?
options: A novel is divided into short chapters that alternate between two narrators
The writer uses similes that compare the sea to sheets of grey glass
Characters speak in colloquial dialect, dropping the ends of words
The narration stays in present tense verbs throughout the story
questions.explanation: Text structure refers to how a whole text is organised and sequenced — chapter division, ordering of events, alternating narrators, framing devices. The tempting choice is the similes comparing the sea to grey glass, but figurative comparisons operate at word and phrase level, so they are language features (literary devices), not structure. A useful cue: if you could only notice it by looking at the shape of the whole text, it is structure; if you notice it in a single sentence, it is a language feature.

questions.stem: In film and picture books, what does a 'low camera angle' looking up at a character most typically encourage an audience to feel about that character?
options: That the character is being honest with the other characters
That the character is remembering something from the past
That the character has power or dominance in the scene
That the character is weak and needs the audience's pity
questions.explanation: Camera angle positions the viewer physically, and that physical position carries meaning: looking up at a figure makes it loom, suggesting power, authority or threat. The option about weakness and pity reverses this — that effect comes from a high angle looking down, which makes a figure appear small. The cue is to ask where the viewer's eye has been placed: below a subject means the subject towers over us.

questions.stem: In a novel, one group of characters is repeatedly described using words such as 'swarmed', 'infested' and 'nest'. What is this pattern of word choice most clearly doing to the reader's response?
options: Showing the reader that the group lives in a crowded city
Proving that the narrator is a scientist by training
Suggesting the group will win the conflict in the end
Encouraging the reader to see that group as less than human
questions.explanation: Repeated animal or insect vocabulary is a connotation pattern, and its effect is dehumanising: the reader is nudged towards viewing the group as a mass rather than as individuals, which is an ethical position the text builds. The 'crowded city' option mistakes the literal meaning of the words for their connotation — the point is not where the group lives but how the language frames them. Look for repeated word families and ask what attitude they carry, not what they describe.

questions.stem: A documentary about land clearing ends by holding a long, silent shot on a single burnt tree before the credits. What is the most likely purpose of this closing image?
options: To signal that the rest of the film should be understood as fiction
To leave the audience sitting with the loss so they adopt the film's position
To confirm to the audience that the events shown were filmed recently
To show the audience that the film-makers ran out of footage
questions.explanation: Duration and silence are moving-image choices: withholding sound and cutting away slowly forces reflection, which is how a documentary invites viewers to take up its ethical stance. The option about proving recency is tempting because documentaries do use footage as evidence, but a lingering shot conveys feeling, not a date. Ask what a shot's length and soundtrack do to your feelings, not what facts they prove.

questions.stem: A short story is narrated in first person by a soldier who describes the enemy only through a rifle sight. How does this narrative choice most affect the reader's ethical position?
options: It removes any bias from the story because the reader sees events directly
It forces the reader to sympathise equally with both sides of the conflict
It restricts the reader to one viewpoint, making it harder to sympathise with the enemy
It makes the reader trust every judgement the narrator makes as objective fact
questions.explanation: Point of view controls access: a limited first-person narrator gives the reader only one character's field of vision and feeling, so the people outside it remain distant and the reader's sympathy is channelled. The option claiming there is no bias because we see events directly is the most tempting, but immediacy is not neutrality — seeing through one pair of eyes is the bias. Ask whose eyes and whose feelings you are denied access to.

questions.stem: A film shows a young shoplifter twice: first in a shaky handheld shot from a security camera's height, then later in a still, close-up shot of her face as she explains her situation. What is the best explanation of this pairing?
options: The shift shows the audience that the second scene is imaginary
The shift proves that handheld camera work is unsuitable for serious films
The shift indicates that the two scenes involve two different characters
The shift in framing moves the audience from judging her to understanding her
questions.explanation: Framing controls distance: surveillance-style distance invites suspicion, while a sustained close-up on a face invites empathy, so the sequence deliberately repositions the audience's ethical judgement. The 'imaginary' option is tempting because a change in visual style can mark a dream, but nothing here signals unreality — only a change in how close we are allowed to get. Track whether a change in shot alters your distance from a character or the story's reality.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how a text can shape a reader's social or ethical position?
options: Through the reader's existing opinions alone, since texts cannot influence anyone
Through accumulated language and image choices that make some responses feel natural
Only through statements the narrator makes directly to the reader about right and wrong
Only when the writer belongs to the same social group as the characters described
questions.explanation: Positioning usually works by accumulation: word choice, point of view, colour, sound and framing build up until one response feels obvious and others feel odd. The option restricting influence to direct narratorial statements is tempting because such statements are the easiest to spot, but most positioning is implied rather than stated. When analysing, look for repeated patterns of choice rather than a single sentence of moral comment.

questions.stem: When analysing a still image in a graphic novel or picture book, the term 'salience' refers to:
options: the symbolic meaning traditionally attached to particular colours in a culture
the element the eye is drawn to first because of its size, colour, contrast or placement
the caption or written text placed underneath the image to explain its meaning
the height of the camera or viewpoint from which the scene has been drawn
questions.explanation: Salience is about visual emphasis: illustrators make one part of an image stand out through scale, colour intensity, sharp contrast or position so the audience notices it first, which steers how they read the scene. The option about camera or viewpoint height describes angle, a different technique that shapes power and sympathy rather than what is noticed first. Cue: salience answers 'what pulls my eye?', while angle answers 'where am I looking from?'

questions.stem: What is an intertextual reference in a literary text?
options: A footnote giving the source of a factual claim in a text
A deliberate echo of, or pointer to, another text within a new text
A quotation from a review printed at the front of a book
A repeated word or image used within one text for emphasis
questions.explanation: Intertextuality means one text referring to, borrowing from or reworking another text, so readers bring their knowledge of the earlier text to the new one. The option about a repeated word or image within one text describes internal patterning or motif, not intertextuality, because nothing outside the text is invoked. The cue is 'inter' — between texts, not inside one.
questions.teaching:
Texts refer to other texts constantly, and the term for that referring is worth knowing precisely.

It covers deliberate echoes: a quoted line, a borrowed structure, a title alluding to something older, a scene shaped like a famous one. It works only when the audience recognises the earlier text, which is why references to Shakespeare, fairy tales and the Bible are so common — they are the works most readers have in common. Coincidental similarity does not count; the reference has to be doing something deliberate.

questions.stem: A young adult novel is titled 'Something Wicked' and opens with three strange sisters predicting a boy's future. Which earlier text is being referenced?
options: Homer's 'The Odyssey'
Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein'
Charles Dickens' 'Oliver Twist'
Shakespeare's 'Macbeth'
questions.explanation: The three prophesying sisters and the phrase 'something wicked' both come from 'Macbeth', where the witches foretell Macbeth's rise. 'The Odyssey' is tempting because it also involves prophecy and a long-foretold fate, but it has no trio of witches and no matching phrase. Look for the combination of signals — a title phrase plus a distinctive character grouping — rather than a single loose similarity.
questions.teaching:
When a text deliberately echoes an earlier one, readers who recognise the echo get an extra layer of meaning.

Recognising it means spotting the borrowed elements: a distinctive phrase, a famous scene, a character type, a title lifted from a well-known line. Three strange women who predict a man's future is one of the most heavily borrowed setups in English literature, and the phrase 'something wicked' comes from the same play. Working out the reference means asking which earlier work has both of those features together.

questions.stem: A poem about a school swimming carnival describes a boy who 'flew too near the sun and fell'. What new understanding does this reference to the Icarus myth enable?
options: It indicates the poem is set in ancient Greece rather than a modern school
It shows the weather at the carnival was unusually hot and bright
It frames the boy's ambition as dangerous overreaching with an inevitable fall
It suggests the boy's swimming ability is superior to everyone else's
questions.explanation: Icarus ignored warnings, flew too high and fell, so the allusion loads the boy's ambition with warning and doom, reading an ordinary carnival as a small tragedy. The option about superior swimming ability picks up only the flattering half of the myth and ignores the fall, which is the point of the reference. When you meet an allusion, carry across the whole story, especially its ending.

questions.stem: A novel's chapters are each named after a plague from a religious text, and each chapter shows a new disaster in a country town. What does this pattern of intertextual reference most clearly enable a reader to understand?
options: The novel's events are literally caused by supernatural forces in the story world
The author is retelling the earlier text with no changes to plot or characters
The chapter titles are decorative and carry no bearing on the novel's meaning
The town's troubles are being framed as a mounting sequence of punishment or judgement
questions.explanation: Borrowing the plague structure imports its logic of escalating, meaningful affliction, so the reader reads the disasters as judgement rather than bad luck. Saying the events are literally supernatural confuses the frame with the plot — the allusion shapes how we interpret events without changing what physically happens. Test an allusion by asking what interpretive frame it lends, not what it adds to the storyline.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of an intertextual reference in a novel?
options: The narrator describes a coming storm using an extended metaphor about war
The author uses long sentences and semicolons to slow the pace of a scene
The story is set in a real Melbourne suburb that is named in the text
Each chapter begins with a quoted line from a Shakespeare play as an epigraph
questions.explanation: An intertextual reference is a deliberate link inside one text to another text, so quoting lines from a Shakespeare play at the head of each chapter points readers towards that earlier work. The extended metaphor about war is tempting, but a metaphor draws on an idea, not on a particular identifiable text, so it is a language feature rather than intertextuality. The cue: ask whether you could name the other text being pointed to.

questions.stem: Why do writers include intertextual references in literary texts?
options: They invite readers to carry meaning from the earlier text across, adding new layers to the new one
They prove the writer has read widely, which makes the writing more believable to readers
They let the writer skip describing a character, because readers already know that person
They tell readers the ending in advance, which makes a complicated plot easier to follow
questions.explanation: The point of an intertextual reference is that a reader's knowledge of the earlier story, character or line is activated and then applied to the new situation, producing an understanding the new text could not create alone. The idea that the reference saves the writer from describing a character is tempting, but referenced characters are still built in the new text; the reference shades our reading of them rather than replacing the writing. Ask what extra meaning the link creates, not what work it saves.

questions.stem: A play set in a busy office includes a character named Cassandra, who repeatedly warns her colleagues that the company is about to collapse and is brushed aside every time. What new understanding does this reference to Greek myth enable?
options: That the events of the play are supernatural rather than an ordinary workplace story
That she will be revealed as the person responsible for the company's collapse
That her warnings are accurate but doomed to be disbelieved, sharpening the play's theme
That she is manipulating her colleagues with predictions she knows to be untrue
questions.explanation: In Greek myth Cassandra is given true prophecies but cursed so that nobody believes her, so naming this character Cassandra tells an informed reader in advance that she is right and will still be ignored, which is what deepens the play's criticism of the office. The option about manipulation reverses the myth, mistaking disbelief by others for dishonesty by her. The cue: work out what happened to the original figure, then map that pattern onto the new character.

questions.stem: In a short story, a boy who has been shut out by his school friendship group keeps rereading Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein' and starts referring to himself as 'the creature'. What new understanding does this intertextual reference most enable?
options: It signals to readers that the short story is set in the same historical period and country as Shelley's novel
It shows readers that the writer has borrowed a ready-made character and so the story carries no meaning of its own
It invites readers to see his isolation as something produced by others' rejection rather than by anything monstrous in him
It confirms for readers that the boy is genuinely dangerous and will eventually harm his classmates, as the creature does
questions.explanation: An intertextual reference brings the meanings of the earlier text into the new one, so readers can read the boy through what Shelley's creature represents: a being made monstrous by how others treat it. That is the new understanding — his exclusion is imposed on him, not deserved. The tempting option is the one claiming the reference confirms he is dangerous and will harm his classmates; it treats the borrowed figure as a plot prediction rather than a lens on meaning, and it ignores that the creature's violence in Shelley's novel follows rejection. A useful cue: ask what idea the reference lets you see, not what event it lets you guess.

questions.stem: When we say a passage has a 'bitter tone', we are describing:
options: the attitude the narrator or speaker takes towards what is being described
the subject matter that the passage happens to be written about
the number of harsh or unpleasant events that occur in the passage
the reader's own opinion of whether the passage is worth reading
questions.explanation: Tone is the attitude or stance a narrator or speaker takes, conveyed through word choice and sentence patterns — bitter, playful, respectful, and so on. The option about subject matter is the most tempting, but a bitter tone can be used to write about something pleasant, and a neutral tone can describe something terrible, so tone is not the topic. Ask 'how does the speaker seem to feel about this?' rather than 'what is this about?'
questions.teaching:
Two terms describe the emotional dimension of a text and they are constantly swapped, so the useful question is whose feeling is meant.

One describes the writer's or narrator's attitude towards what they are describing — which might be bitter, admiring, amused, or coldly neutral. It shows in word choice and in what gets emphasised or left out. The other describes the atmosphere the reader ends up feeling. Naming a specific emotion like bitterness points at the first, because bitterness is an attitude someone holds rather than an atmosphere.

questions.stem: A student wants a first-person narrator to sound more anxious and rushed, without changing any of the events described. Which revision would best achieve this?
options: join the sentences with semicolons and formal linking words
add several adjectives before each noun so descriptions run longer
break the long sentence into short fragments interrupted by dashes
rewrite the verbs in passive voice so the narrator sounds detached
questions.explanation: Anxiety in a voice is usually built from sentence patterning: clipped fragments and dashes imitate a mind that keeps breaking off and restarting, so the reader hears panic without being told about it. Passive voice is a real technique with a real effect, but that effect is distance and detachment, which is the opposite of anxious urgency. Remember that voice comes from how sentences move, not just from what the words mean.

questions.stem: A poem about drought is packed with hard consonants: 'cracked crust', 'stock tank', 'kicked dust'. What is the best account of this choice?
options: the repeated sounds are there to make the poem easier to learn by heart
the tough consonants signal that the poem should be read as a factual report
the harsh sounds make the lines feel as dry and hard as the land being described
the difficult sounds show the poet lacked softer words for describing a drought
questions.explanation: Sound patterning is part of a poem's aesthetic quality: when the consonants a reader must force out are harsh, the physical experience of reading matches the harshness of the scene, so sound reinforces meaning. The memorisation option confuses sound patterning with rhyme and metre used as memory aids, which is not what these clustered consonants are doing here. Ask what the sounds feel like in your mouth, then check whether that feeling matches the subject.

questions.stem: A chapter is written in long, flowing sentences full of subordinate clauses, and then one line reads simply: 'The house was gone.' What is the main effect of this shift?
options: the short sentence marks the point where the narrative moves into a flashback
the change signals to the reader that spoken dialogue is about to begin
the abrupt short sentence stands out sharply and forces the reader to stop on it
the shift shows that a different narrator has taken over telling the story
questions.explanation: Effects of sentence length are relative: after a run of long sentences, a four-word sentence lands with unusual weight, giving the information emphasis and a flat, stunned tone. The 'different narrator' option mistakes a change in rhythm for a change in speaker — a narrator shift is normally signalled by a new name, heading or clear change in voice and knowledge. Look for contrast with what came just before when judging the effect of any sentence pattern.

questions.stem: A poem about a grandmother describes her hands as 'creased like a folded map', her wrists as 'dry creek beds' and her knuckles as 'stones the flood left behind'. What is the best account of this sustained pattern of imagery?
options: It shows the poet ran out of ideas, since three comparisons are used where one clear description would do
It tells the reader that the grandmother works outdoors, which is the literal information the images supply
It links her ageing body to a worked, weathered landscape, so a life of time and labour is made visible in one figure
It proves the poet is writing about an actual drought rather than about a person, since the images are all about land
questions.explanation: When separate images all draw on the same field — here land shaped slowly by weather and water — they build a single, deepening comparison, and the aesthetic pleasure comes from the reader recognising the connection. The 'works outdoors' option is tempting because it treats each image as literal information; but comparisons tell us how something feels or seems, not what the person's job is. The cue: notice whether the images belong to one shared world, then ask what that world lets you understand about the subject.

questions.stem: In studying literary texts, the term 'imagery' most precisely refers to:
options: the illustrations, maps and cover artwork that a publisher adds to a printed literary text
any use of figurative language, including puns, irony and deliberate understatement
the arrangement of sentences into paragraphs of varying length across a chapter
language that appeals to the senses so a reader can picture, hear or feel what is described
questions.explanation: Imagery is sensory language: writers choose words (often with simile or metaphor) that make a reader see, hear, smell, taste or feel something, which is how imagery builds meaning and aesthetic quality. The option about puns, irony and understatement is tempting because those are also literary devices, but they work through double meaning or tone, not through appeals to the senses. The cue is the word 'image' — ask whether the language creates a sensory experience in the reader's mind rather than just a clever verbal effect.

questions.stem: A first-person narrator describes arriving at a new school: 'Was I early? Were they staring? Had I said something wrong already? Why was my bag so loud?' What does this pattern of sentences most contribute to the narrator's voice?
options: It signals a change of setting, because question sentences are used to mark time passing
It makes the voice sound uncertain and self-conscious, caught up in worry about being judged
It makes the voice sound authoritative, because the narrator is questioning other characters directly
It shows the narration has shifted from first person to an all-knowing third-person narrator
questions.explanation: A run of unanswered questions with no statements gives the reader only the narrator's anxious guessing, so the voice reads as unsure and hyper-aware of being watched. The 'authoritative' option misreads who the questions are aimed at: these are the narrator's private thoughts, not challenges put to other people, and interrogating oneself undercuts authority rather than asserting it. Check who the question is addressed to — questions turned inward build doubt, while questions aimed at others can build power.

questions.stem: When planning a short story, a writer decides to include images of locked doors in several different chapters. In literary terms, this repeated element is best described as a:
options: simile
stanza
synonym
motif
questions.explanation: A motif is an image, object or idea that recurs across a text, building meaning through repetition — here, locked doors gathering associations of secrecy or entrapment. 'Simile' is the tempting choice because it also involves images, but a simile is a single explicit comparison using 'like' or 'as', not a pattern of repetition. The cue is repetition across a whole text: one comparison is a simile, a returning image is a motif.
questions.teaching:
A single striking image is one thing; the same image returning again and again is something else, and the difference is repetition.

When an image, object or idea recurs across a text, it starts to accumulate meaning — each appearance colours the ones before and after it. That is what turns it into a structural device rather than a detail. It is closely related to a symbol, which is a single thing standing for a larger idea, and the two overlap; the distinguishing feature here is that it appears repeatedly rather than once.

questions.stem: A student wants to use personification in a description of an empty kitchen at night. Which sentence does this?
options: I have told you a thousand times to lock up.
The old fridge sulked in the corner all night.
The dam outside was as flat as a sheet of glass.
The back gate clanged and rattled in the wind.
questions.explanation: Personification gives human qualities, feelings or actions to something non-human, so a fridge that 'sulked' is personified. The gate that 'clanged and rattled' is tempting, but those words imitate sounds, which makes them onomatopoeia rather than human behaviour. Ask whether the object is doing something only a person could feel or choose to do — sulking yes, rattling no.
questions.teaching:
Giving human qualities to something that is not human is a specific device, and the test is what is being described.

The subject has to be non-human — an object, an animal, a place, an abstract idea — and it has to be doing something only a person can do: sulking, complaining, waiting, refusing. If the sentence describes a person behaving like a person, nothing figurative is happening. If it compares one thing to another using 'like' or 'as', that is a different device. Look for the non-human subject with a human verb.

questions.stem: In a piece of creative writing, a student places a description of a birthday party directly beside a description of a funeral in the next paragraph. This technique is called:
options: juxtaposition
alliteration
hyperbole
apostrophe
questions.explanation: Juxtaposition means positioning two contrasting elements side by side so that each sharpens the reader's sense of the other. 'Hyperbole' tempts students because both feel like devices that heighten an effect, but hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration within a description, not the arrangement of two contrasting parts. If the effect comes from placement and contrast rather than from the words themselves, it is juxtaposition.
questions.teaching:
Placing two very different things side by side makes a reader see both more sharply, and the technique has a name.

Nothing is compared explicitly and no connecting word is used — the contrast does the work simply by proximity. A celebration next to a funeral, wealth next to poverty, calm next to violence. Writers use it to force a comparison the reader makes for themselves, which is more persuasive than stating it. It is a structural device rather than a figure of speech, so it operates at the level of what is placed where.

questions.stem: A student's draft reads: 'The abandoned mine felt dangerous and scary.' She wants to create that feeling through a literary device instead of stating it. Which revision does that?
options: 'She was scared of the mine because mines are genuinely dangerous.'
'The mine, which was dangerous and scary, was where she stood.'
'The mine shaft breathed cold air onto the back of her neck.'
'The mine was a dangerous, scary place that frightened her badly.'
questions.explanation: Using personification — the shaft 'breathed' — makes the reader experience the threat through an image rather than being told the label, which is the point of experimenting with devices for effect. The version listing 'dangerous, scary... frightened her badly' is tempting because it sounds more emphatic, but adding more evaluative adjectives is still telling the reader the conclusion. Check whether the reader is given something to picture or simply a judgement to accept.

questions.stem: A student wants to use sibilance so that a night-time scene sounds hushed and secretive. Which line best achieves this?
options: 'The gate banged, then banged again, then banged once more.'
'Her heart beat like a drum in a marching band parade.'
'She slipped past the sleeping house, silent as spilled sand.'
'The cracked tin bucket kicked back against the concrete step.'
questions.explanation: Sibilance is the repetition of soft 's' and 'sh' sounds, and the hissing, whispered quality of those sounds suits a hushed, secretive mood. The line with 'cracked', 'kicked' and 'concrete' is the trap: it does repeat sounds, but they are hard plosive consonants, which create harshness rather than hush. Identify which consonant is repeated before naming the effect.

questions.stem: A student begins a reflective piece with: 'Exam week rolled in like weather.' Which next sentence best sustains this as an extended metaphor?
options: 'What I mean is that exam week made all of us feel very tense indeed.'
'My friend Nadia had studied for weeks and was not worried about it.'
'By Wednesday the pressure had dropped and everyone spoke in low thunder.'
'Exam week was also like a battlefield, with soldiers falling on all sides.'
questions.explanation: An extended metaphor develops one comparison across several sentences, so continuing with weather language — pressure dropping, low thunder — keeps the single controlling image alive. The battlefield sentence is tempting because it is also figurative, but switching to an unrelated comparison creates a mixed metaphor and breaks the pattern. Test each new sentence by asking whether it still belongs to the first image's world.

questions.stem: In one paragraph a student compares the same river to a snake, a ribbon, a wound, a rope and a mirror. What is the most accurate account of this experiment?
options: It is an extended metaphor, because every comparison is about the same river.
It is personification, because the river is being given a body and a shape.
It becomes a motif, because the river is mentioned five times in the paragraph.
The comparisons compete, so the reader cannot hold one clear image of the river.
questions.explanation: Figurative language works by directing the reader to one controlling image; five unrelated comparisons in quick succession cancel each other out and draw attention to the writing rather than the river. Calling it an extended metaphor is the most tempting error, but an extended metaphor sustains and develops a single comparison — here each simile abandons the last. Remember that a motif recurs across a whole text, and personification requires human qualities, not just physical shapes.

questions.stem: A writer wants a first-person narrator whose account lets the reader realise something the narrator herself has not worked out. Which drafting choice best creates that gap?
options: Have her report small details plainly, without explaining what they mean.
Have her admit at the end that she had misread the situation all along.
Have her describe her feelings at length whenever something confuses her.
Rewrite the piece in third person so the truth can be stated outright.
questions.explanation: The gap between narrator and reader depends on the narrator supplying evidence but not the interpretation, so the reader assembles a meaning she misses. Having her admit her mistake at the end is tempting because it acknowledges the misreading, but once she names it the gap closes and the reader learns nothing ahead of her. The cue is who does the interpreting: leave that work to the reader and the irony survives.
